data.title: Parry–Romberg syndrome — viva
data.summary: Connective tissue diseases · 9 viva questions with answers
data.body:
_Viva questions for the case: **Parry–Romberg syndrome** (Connective tissue diseases)_

**Q1. What is Parry–Romberg syndrome? (PYQ)**
- Progressive hemifacial atrophy — slowly progressive, usually unilateral atrophy of the skin, subcutaneous fat, muscle and bone of the face, typically in the distribution of one or more branches of the trigeminal nerve; considered part of the linear morphoea spectrum (often coexists with en coup de sabre)

**Q2. Clinical features.**
- Onset in childhood/adolescence (first or second decade), females more
- Progressive sinking of one side of face — cheek, temple, around eye (enophthalmos), lip, tongue, gums; minimal skin induration (unlike en coup de sabre), sometimes hyperpigmentation; deviation of mouth and nose to affected side
- Progression for 2–10 years then 'burns out'
- Associated: ipsilateral hair loss/whitening, heterochromia of iris, uveitis, dental root atrophy, delayed eruption, trigeminal neuralgia, facial pain, migraine, seizures (with intracranial calcification or white-matter lesions on MRI)

**Q3. How do you differentiate it from en coup de sabre?**
- En coup de sabre: paramedian forehead/frontal scalp linear band, sclerotic/indurated skin, scarring alopecia
- Parry–Romberg: lower face (below forehead), atrophy of deeper tissues predominantly with little skin sclerosis
- Both may coexist and share neurological complications

**Q4. Investigations.**
- MRI brain (ipsilateral white-matter hyperintensities, calcification, atrophy) and EEG if neurological symptoms; ophthalmology review
- Facial imaging (CT/MRI) to assess bone/fat loss; photographs and measurements to track progression
- ANA, anti-ssDNA (may be positive)

**Q5. Differential diagnosis.**
- Linear morphoea/en coup de sabre, facial lipodystrophy (HIV/acquired partial lipodystrophy — bilateral), Rasmussen encephalitis, lupus profundus, hemifacial microsomia (congenital, non-progressive), steroid-induced lipoatrophy, Barraquer–Simons syndrome (bilateral, cephalocaudal)

**Q6. Management.**
- Active phase: methotrexate with systemic corticosteroids (pulse methylprednisolone) as in linear morphoea; mycophenolate; hydroxychloroquine (adjunct)
- After disease is inactive (≥1–2 years stable): reconstructive surgery — autologous fat grafting (most common), dermal fillers (hyaluronic acid), free flaps, bone grafts/implants; orthodontic and dental care
- Antiepileptics for seizures; eye care

**Q7. Prognosis.**
- Self-limiting progression with permanent facial asymmetry; psychosocial impact large

**Q8. What scoring helps follow the disease?**
- Serial standardised photographs, 3D imaging/ facial measurements, LoSCAT (modified Localised Scleroderma Skin Severity Index and Damage Index), MRI of face/brain for deep and neurological activity

**Q9. What dental and ocular complications occur?**
- Dental: root resorption, delayed eruption, malocclusion, jaw hypoplasia on affected side
- Ocular: enophthalmos, uveitis, heterochromia, eyelid atrophy, retinal vasculitis, optic neuritis — need ophthalmic follow-up

## Quick spotter facts
- Unilateral progressive facial sinking in a child without much skin sclerosis — Parry–Romberg
- Treat active phase like linear morphoea; reconstruct after burnout

_Sources: Previous-year PG question papers (Sahana P Raju, Solved Papers Dermatology); IADVL Textbook of Dermatology 5e (Morphoea — progressive hemifacial atrophy). Answers written in our own words; check with your teachers' preferences._
